name: Romandalusí / Andalusi Romance
catalog_citation: Corriente, Federico. 2000-2001. "El romandalusí reflejado por el glosario botánico de Abulxayr." Estudios de Dialectología Norteafricana y Andalusí (EDNA) 5: 93-241.
catalog_locator: p. 229, 'Esquema gramatical', sec. 1.3 'Fonemas suprasegmentales', 1.3.1 (saved file = galley 3, page image 37; scanned)
catalog_quote: 1.3.1. El acento tónico, fuertemente espiratorio, del romand., actúa del modo previsible en estos materiales, ocasionando frecuentes caídas de vocales, e incluso sílabas enteras, pretónicas (vgr., BICTINÁČ < pastĭnaca, DONNEQÁL < dŏmĭnĭcālis, MAQÁRČA < *MAṬREQALEČA, etc.) o postónicas (vgr., ČERBÍNNA < *ČÉRKO ḌE PÉNNA, QOḌQÁWČE < *QOḌA ḌE QÁWČE, etc.), aunque conocemos insuficientemente este haz dialectal para saber porqué esto no ocurre siempre (vgr., BERḌELÁQAS, BERTEČÉḶO, ĠARIṬÁYRA, etc., tal vez a causa de una mayor debilidad de dicho acento en algunas circunstancias. El acento es etimológico, desde luego, y no se desplaza, contra lo que ha veces se ha afirmado, sino a los sufijos tónicos, inflexionales o derivacionales.

new_statements.translation: 1.3.1. The tonic stress of Andalusi Romance, strongly expiratory, behaves as expected in these materials, causing frequent loss of pretonic vowels and even whole syllables (e.g. BICTINÁČ < pastinaca, DONNEQÁL < dominicalis, MAQÁRČA < *MATREQALEČA, etc.) or post-tonic ones (e.g. ČERBÍNNA < *ČÉRKO DE PÉNNA ...), although we know this dialect bundle too poorly to say why this does not always happen (e.g. BERDELÁQAS, BERTEČÉLO, ĠARITÁYRA, etc.), perhaps because of a greater weakness of that stress in some circumstances. The stress is etymological, of course, and does not shift—contrary to what has sometimes been claimed—except onto tonic suffixes, inflectional or derivational.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is a strong dynamic (expiratory) stress that stays on the syllable that bore it in the Latin etymon (i.e. the inherited, lexically fixed Latin penult/antepenult position, surfacing as penult, antepenult or—after apocope, e.g. DONNEQÁL, BICTINÁČ—final); it is not displaced by Arabic influence; stressed ('tonic') inflectional and derivational suffixes (diminutive, -ÁČ, etc.) take the stress when added.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress moves only onto tonic suffixes (inflectional or derivational); occasional distortion of stress in rhyme position in the kharjas (Corriente 1995: 13, 1.3.1); a few learned/contaminated items with anti-etymological stress are discussed individually in the lexicon (e.g. ABRÉQANO, cappáris, íberus); Corriente (p. 102 n. 93) explicitly rejects Galmés de Fuentes 1983: 279's claim of a general Arabic-induced shift to the antepenult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; evidence is the plene/defective spelling of vowels (matres lectionis mark the stressed vowel) in Arabic-script transcriptions of isolated Romance plant names and phrases (citation forms), 11th-12th c., plus kharja verse.
new_statements.identity_note: Corriente's "romandalusí" (Andalusi Romance) is the same entity Glottolog calls Mozarabic [moza1249] (ISO mxi); Corriente explicitly rejects the label "mozárabe". The 2000-01 statement rests on the Romance botanical vocabulary transmitted in Arabic script in the glossary of the Sevillian agronomist Abū-l-Khayr (ʿUmdat al-ṭabīb, 11th-12th c.), supplemented by the kharjas (Corriente 1995, 1997); it describes a 'haz dialectal' (dialect bundle) of al-Andalus, 9th-12th c., not a single local variety.
